full_story_objects.headline: The whole of Georgia lost power for nine hours

sources.title: Georgia plunges into darkness as rare nationwide blackout hits
Georgia hit by nationwide power outage

chunks.text: The lights {{went out}} across the whole of Georgia at about 00:10 on July 24. Tbilisi, Kutaisi and the [[breakaway]] region of Abkhazia all lost power [[at once]]. Georgian State Electrosystem, the national [[grid]] operator, said an emergency [[shutdown]] had caused it and that supply would return [[in stages]]. Power was fully [[restored]] at about 09:30, more than nine hours later, but the official cause is still unknown.

verbs.correct: To stop shining or working, as a light does
verbs.wrong: To be officially approved or passed

chunks.text: A national grid works as one machine, with [[supply and demand]] held in balance second by second. If a large plant or line fails, automatic protection {{kicks in}} and disconnects equipment to [[prevent]] damage, and the loss can {{knock out}} the rest of the system in seconds. In April 2025 a shutdown of the Kavkasioni [[transmission line]] left about 90 percent of [[consumers]] without power.

verbs.correct: To start to work or take effect
verbs.wrong: To create a lot of noise or fuss

verbs.correct: To make something stop working

chunks.text: The energy ministry in Abkhazia blamed a system failure at the Enguri [[hydropower]] plant, which supplies both Abkhazia and territory held by Georgia's central government. Tbilisi did not comment on that [[account]]. The grid operator said the exact causes were still being established. It also {{called on}} news organizations to [[rely on]] official information, saying false claims were [[circulating]]. No explanation has yet been [[confirmed]].

chunks.text: Several Tbilisi metro trains stopped inside tunnels on the night's last services, and the Tbilisi Transport Company said every passenger {{got out}} safely. Georgian Water and Power said its [[pumping stations]] {{shut down}} automatically, putting water supply [[at risk]] in Tbilisi and Rustavi, though the company said the night passed with [[minimal]] problems. Power {{came back on}} area by area, reaching parts of the capital and Kutaisi by 02:09. The rest of the country spent the night in the dark.

full_story_objects.headline: France bans social media for children under 15

sources.title: French parliament passes social media ban for under-15s
French parliament passes social media ban for young teens

chunks.text: France's parliament voted on July 21 to [[bar]] children under 15 from social media and to ban mobile phones in schools. Both [[chambers]] [[backed]] it, making France the first European Union country to approve such a ban. It is not law yet. The Constitutional Council, which checks new laws against the [[constitution]], must still {{sign off on}} the text, and that could {{push back}} the start date.

verbs.correct: To give official approval to something
verbs.wrong: To transfer legal ownership to someone else

verbs.correct: To delay something to a later time
verbs.wrong: To force a new law through parliament

chunks.text: The law arrives [[in two stages]]. From September 1, 2026, [[platforms]] such as TikTok, Snapchat and Instagram must stop under-15s from {{signing up}}. [[Accounts]] they already have will be closed from January 2027. Educational and scientific sites are [[exempt]] from the ban. That means [[age checks]] for almost everyone: adults will also have to prove their age when they {{log in}}. The checking tools must be approved by the national privacy regulator, the body that [[guards]] personal data.

chunks.text: Gaelle Berbonde, a parent who [[campaigned]] for the [[bill]], said families had {{run out of}} options. "The only thing we can do is protect our children, just as we protect our children from drinking alcohol," she said. President Emmanuel Macron called the vote "[[a major step forward]]" and said France was [[leading the way]] in Europe.

verbs.correct: To have no more of something left

chunks.text: Lawmakers from the left-wing France Unbowed party voted against it, arguing the ban may not {{stand up}} in court, that it cannot be [[enforced]], and that making everyone prove their age would {{do away with}} [[anonymity]] online. The text sets no [[penalties]] for children, parents or platforms, which leaves [[enforcement]] [[unclear]]. Australia already bars under-16s, and the European Union is expected to {{put forward}} its own bill in the fall. For French families, the first test comes with the new school year.

chunks.text: Vozinha, Cape Verde's [[goalkeeper]], is 40. On June 15, 2026, in his country's first World Cup match, his team {{took on}} Spain, one of the [[favorites]], and held them to a 0-0 draw. Afterward he explained that his mother, Ana Candida Evora, could not get a US [[visa]] and had {{stayed behind}}. Two days later that changed.

Most people {{found out}} only when Vozinha mentioned it after the match, and the interview spread within hours. On June 17, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and State Department officials waived the [[fees]], and Cape Verde's government and FIFA {{stepped in}} [[as well]].

chunks.text: Hakeem Jeffries, the House Democratic leader, announced it, thanking Rubio, State Department officials, Cape Verde's government and FIFA "for working together to make this possible." The clip was watched [[widely]], and Uzbekistan's team invited him to training, where players gave him a signed shirt and a toy wolf. Evora reached the tournament for a similar reason: strangers {{took up}} her case until officials acted. On June 21 she {{looked on}} from the [[stands]] in Miami as her son played at a World Cup [[for the first time]].

His words {{set off}} worry among the [[allies]] who had [[gathered]], because a wider conflict could [[spread]] across the region.

tf.s: In court, one man owned up to several thefts from the warehouse.
tf.why: The man owned up to the thefts, which means he admitted that he had done them.

tf.s: The stolen portrait turned up next to cash and drugs during the raid.
tf.why: The portrait turned up, which means it was found, next to the cash and drugs in the house.

tf.s: Police officers came across the stolen Picasso while searching the house.
tf.why: Police came across the painting, which means they found it by chance during the drug raid.

tf.s: The security guard gave back the painting while he worked at the warehouse.
tf.why: The guard made off with the painting, which means he stole it. Give back means to return something to its owner, the opposite of what he did.

tf.s: Police said the valuable Picasso will be taken away from its owner.
tf.why: Police said the painting will be given back to its owner, meaning returned to them. Take away means to remove something, the opposite of returning it.

full_story_objects.headline: A 1,000-year-old Viking workshop is found in Denmark

sources.title: Spectacular find: 1,000-year-old Viking textile workshop unearthed (Euronews)
Archaeologists find huge Viking textile production site in Denmark (NPR)
Archaeologists Find Industrial-Scale Viking Textile Hub In Denmark (Forbes)
A huge Viking textile production site is unearthed in Denmark (video, AP Archive)

chunks.text: [[Archaeologists]] in Denmark have {{dug up}} about 82 pit houses near the city of Aarhus. They say the buildings once {{made up}} a large Viking workshop where people produced cloth. The houses {{date back}} to a period between the 7th and 10th centuries. Experts from the Moesgaard Museum {{carried out}} a ten-month [[excavation]] at Soften, a village just north of Aarhus.

verbs.wrong: To build a house or wall out of wood and stone
verbs.correct: To remove something from the ground by digging

verbs.wrong: To be built close together
verbs.correct: To form or be the parts of something

verbs.wrong: To be older than anything else in the area
verbs.correct: To have existed since a particular time in the past

verbs.wrong: To lead a team of many workers
verbs.correct: To do or complete a task

chunks.text: The team {{found out}} that the site [[covered]] about 100,000 square meters, [[far bigger than]] a normal [[settlement]] would need. Workers there processed [[flax]] and turned it into thread and cloth. Archaeologists {{turned up}} many [[loom weights and spindle whorls]], which are small tools used to spin and [[weave]]. These finds point to [[skilled]] [[craft]] work on an industrial [[scale]], the experts say.

verbs.wrong: To measure something very carefully
verbs.correct: To learn or discover a fact

verbs.wrong: To collect objects and store them safely
verbs.correct: To be found or appear, often by chance

chunks.text: The Vikings did not use all of this cloth themselves. Instead, they {{built up}} a [[wide]] trade network and sold their goods [[far away]]. Some of the [[coins]] [[discovered]] at the site came from present-day France and Germany. The museum says Arabic coins from the Middle East also add to the picture of [[long-distance]] trade.

verbs.wrong: To make an agreement with another country
verbs.correct: To develop or increase something over time

chunks.text: This discovery points to a [[well-organized]] [[society]], not a wild and backward one, historian Kasper Andersen said. Researchers will now {{look into}} the thousands of objects they collected to learn more. It may take several years to {{find out}} [[exactly how]] the [[artifacts]] were made. Even so, the workshop has already helped experts {{set up}} a new picture of how Vikings ran large craft centers.

verbs.correct: To examine or investigate something

verbs.wrong: To test old objects in a laboratory
verbs.correct: To learn or discover a fact

verbs.correct: To create or establish something new

tf.s: Researchers will now set up the thousands of objects to learn more about them.
tf.why: The researchers will look into the objects (examine and study them). Set up means to create or arrange something new, which is not what they will do.

tf.s: Archaeologists dug up about 82 pit houses near Aarhus.
tf.why: This is correct. The archaeologists dug up the pit houses, meaning they removed them from the ground by digging.

tf.s: The experts carried out a ten-month excavation at Soften.
tf.why: This is correct. Carry out means to do or complete a task, and the experts completed a ten-month excavation.

tf.s: Archaeologists set up about 82 pit houses near Aarhus.
tf.why: The archaeologists dug up the pit houses (removed them from the ground). Set up means to build or establish something, which is not what the archaeologists did.

tf.s: The houses date back to a period between the 7th and 10th centuries.
tf.why: This is correct. Date back means to have existed since a time in the past, and the houses are from the 7th to 10th centuries.

tf.s: The Vikings found out a wide trade network and sold their goods far away.
tf.why: The Vikings built up a wide trade network (developed it over time). Find out means to discover a fact, which does not fit here.
